designs.title: Humpback Whale
designs.why: The fin count is wrong: there is a big dorsal-side fin halfway along the back plus two flippers, while a humpback has a tiny dorsal knob near the tail and two very long pectorals, so it reads as a generic whale with an extra limb.

designs.title: Ammonite
designs.why: The inner coil is convincing, but the outer body chamber melts into a lumpy, sagging lobe at lower left, with ribs that fork at random and no suture lines, so it's not yet a real fossil plate.

designs.title: Gaff Cutter
designs.why: It's labelled 'Sail plan' but it's a perspective sketch with tangled, made-up rigging and overlapping headsails, far from the clean elevation of the sailboat reference tee.

designs.title: Hot Air Balloon
designs.why: A believable Montgolfier-style elevation with the load lines meeting at a ring above the basket, though the flame-like smudges on the lower envelope are decoration rather than structure.

designs.title: Scooter
designs.why: The center stand looks like two separate legs, there's a fake 'R' badge, and the smooth grey airbrush shading will turn into a flat 30 lpi dot mush instead of reading as line illustration.

designs.title: Colonial House
designs.why: The closest match to the colonial-building reference: dense, with columns and balconies that stack credibly over three floors, but the soft fade at the edges will halftone into a fuzzy rectangle.

designs.title: Lighthouse
designs.why: Clean, plausible construction (gallery, lantern, staggered stair windows, door and steps), and it really is close to an elevation.

designs.title: Luna Moth
designs.why: The antennae are thin and butterfly-like when a luna's are feathery, the hindwings lack their eyespots, the forewings are shaped like hindwings, and the twisted tails look melted, so a lepidopterist would reject it.

designs.title: Sunflower
designs.why: An honest botanical plate (alternate serrated leaves, a side bud, a believable head), and the 'Flower and leaf' subtitle is accurate.

designs.title: Compass
designs.why: The hinge, bail and graduated dial make mechanical sense, but it's an open three-quarter view, not the 'Front view' the title claims, and the rose has no cardinal letters.

designs.title: Rangefinder Camera
designs.why: A true flat front elevation with plausible Leica-style top-plate dials and windows, but the lens ring lettering is fake, the scale line under the body is detached, and the dark leatherette is heavy at 30 lpi.

designs.title: Red Deer
designs.why: Anatomy and antlers are good, but the lower legs suddenly turn white and hollow below the hocks and knees, a conversion artefact that makes the stag look like it's standing on stilts.

designs.title: Grey Heron
designs.why: Head, plumes and wing are well drawn, but the legs switch from dark to blank white mid-tibia and the feet disappear into a shapeless blob, the same broken-leg artefact as the deer.

suggestions: Do a true orthographic bicycle or penny-farthing patent elevation with a correct wheel and spoke count, chainring and fork, closer to the bicycle reference than the perspective objects in this run.
Make whale or fish study sheets with a main figure plus two or three small views (fluke from below, flipper, skull), so 'study' means a real plate and not one dramatic pose.
Draw a schooner or ketch as a strict side elevation with countable stays and shrouds and a waterline, and only call it a 'Sail plan' when it is one.
Do beetle or crab specimen plates in dorsal view, where six legs or ten legs and their segments can be counted and checked before release.
Add a mandatory leg, foot and antenna check plus a no-fade-to-white rule: subjects need solid, finished extremities and a hard edge, never a soft vignette that halftones into mush.
overall: A solid run of objects and architecture (house, lighthouse, sunflower, camera), but every animal fails on anatomy or extremity artefacts (an extra fin, a wrong moth, legs vanishing into white), and some subtitles ('Sail plan', 'Front view') aren't true. Fix those before calling anything a study.
